question: If PR and PB denote prices for the reference and base periods, then simple index number is given by:
solution:
The correct answer is** PRPB.100" id="MathJax-Element-622-Frame" role="presentation" style="position: relative;" tabindex="0">PRPB.100PRPB.100
\rm \frac{P_R}{P_B}.100
**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__** Explanation:

__
 
• Option 3: PRPB.100" id="MathJax-Element-623-Frame" role="presentation" style="position: relative;" tabindex="0">PRPB.100PRPB.100
 \rm \frac{P_R}{P_B}.100
 - This formula correctly represents the simple price index number. It is calculated by dividing the reference period price (PR) by the base period price (PB) and then multiplying by 100 to convert it into a percentage. 
 
• A simple index number measures the relative change in price over time, making this the correct approach.
 
• This method is widely used to compare prices between two different periods.

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] Important Points__**

 
• **Option 1: (PR + PB).100 - This is incorrect because it adds the prices of the reference and base periods, which does not reflect the change in price.**
 
• **This formula does not provide any meaningful information about the price change between the two periods.**
 
• **The addition of prices and multiplication by 100 is not a standard method for calculating index numbers.**

 
• **Option 2: PBPR.100" id="MathJax-Element-624-Frame" role="presentation" style="position: relative;" tabindex="0">PBPR.100PBPR.100
 \rm \frac{P_B}{P_R}.100
 - This is incorrect because it inverts the reference and base period prices.**
 
• **This would measure the change relative to the reference period, not the base period.**
 
• **It does not reflect the correct direction of comparison for a simple price index.**

 
• **Option 4: PR.PB.100 - This is incorrect because it multiplies the prices of the reference and base periods.**
 
• **Multiplying prices and then multiplying by 100 does not provide a meaningful measure of price change.**
 
• **This formula does not conform to any standard method for calculating price index numbers.**
